title: Exploration
text:
Exploration has an order. First I learn what a row represents, then I establish how quantity behaves on its own, compare it across useful groups, and only then choose graphs. In this dataset, quantity is units of one menu item recorded on one date. Adding items together by date gives a different outcome: total restaurant demand per day. I keep those measures separate so the comparisons stay clear.
The exploration below uses the selected restaurant R07 in Minneapolis and the eight source tables needed for this project. The R code for each step is available in a Show R code dropdown.

title: Exploration
section: Step 1: know what the data describe
text:
Step 1: know what the data describe
Before deciding on a chart, I need to understand the sales table’s structure and what the supporting tables add. The sales table describes item-days; the menu table supplies item names, categories, and listed prices; the calendar adds weekday and month; and the remaining tables support the later questions about cost, weather, events, and marketing.


Show R code
if (data_ready) {
  # Join the two tables needed for item-level exploration, then keep a clean
  # version for summaries while preserving sales with missing quantities.
  sales_menu_all <- sales |>
    left_join(
      menu_items |> select(menu_item_id, menu_item_name, category, unit_price),
      by = "menu_item_id"
    )
  item_day_data <- sales_menu_all |> filter(!is.na(quantity))

  glimpse(sales)

  inventory <- qsr_data_inventory(qsr_data) |>
    transmute(
      `Source table` = table,
      Rows = scales::comma(rows),
      Columns = columns,
      `Missing cells` = scales::comma(missing_cells)
    )

  missing_quantity_count <- sum(is.na(sales$quantity))
  duplicate_item_days <- sales |>
    count(date, menu_item_id) |>
    filter(n > 1) |>
    nrow()
  missing_menu_names <- sum(is.na(sales_menu_all$menu_item_name))
  quality_checks <- tibble(
    Check = c(
      "Missing quantity values",
      "Duplicate date + menu-item combinations",
      "Menu names missing after joining"
    ),
    Result = c(
      paste0(scales::comma(missing_quantity_count), " (",
             scales::number(100 * missing_quantity_count / nrow(sales), accuracy = 0.1), "%)"),
      scales::comma(duplicate_item_days),
      scales::comma(missing_menu_names)
    )
  )

  print(knitr::kable(
    inventory,
    caption = "The eight source tables available to the analysis",
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r")
  ))
  print(knitr::kable(
    quality_checks,
    caption = "Data checks that affect item-day comparisons",
    align = c("l", "r")
  ))
} else {
  cat("Missing source files in data/: ", paste(missing_inputs, collapse = ", "))
}

title: Exploration
section: Step 2: understand the outcome on its own
text:
Step 2: understand the outcome on its own
I start with a baseline before comparing categories or promotions. The table below summarizes both item-day quantity and total daily restaurant demand. The numbers are on different scales, so I label each outcome rather than treating them as interchangeable.


Show R code
if (data_ready) {
  # Daily totals retain the date and sum only the quantities that were recorded.
  daily_demand <- sales |>
    group_by(date) |>
    summarise(
      daily_units = if (all(is.na(quantity))) NA_real_ else sum(quantity, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    left_join(
      calendar |> select(date, day_of_week, day_of_week_num, is_weekend, month, year),
      by = "date"
    )

  item_day_baseline <- item_day_data |>
    summarise(
      Outcome = "Quantity per item-day",
      Observations = n(),
      Mean = mean(quantity),
      Median = median(quantity),
      `90th percentile` = quantile(quantity, 0.90, names = FALSE),
      Maximum = max(quantity),
      .groups = "drop"
    )

  daily_baseline <- daily_demand |>
    summarise(
      Outcome = "Total units per restaurant-day",
      Observations = sum(!is.na(daily_units)),
      Mean = mean(daily_units, na.rm = TRUE),
      Median = median(daily_units, na.rm = TRUE),
      `90th percentile` = quantile(daily_units, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE),
      Maximum = max(daily_units, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    )

  baseline_table <- bind_rows(item_day_baseline, daily_baseline) |>
    mutate(
      Observations = scales::comma(Observations),
      across(c(Mean, Median, `90th percentile`, Maximum), ~ scales::number(.x, accuracy = 0.1))
    )

  knitr::kable(
    baseline_table,
    caption = "Baseline summaries before comparing groups",
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r")
  )
} else {
  cat("Baseline summaries will appear after the eight source CSV files are copied to data/.")
}

For item-level comparisons, rows with missing quantities stay missing instead of being silently converted to zero. Daily totals use the observed quantities on each date, so a date with a missing item quantity can be slightly understated.

What does one item’s daily quantity look like?
One numeric outcome, examined on its own: a histogram. I use the histogram to see the typical range and whether a small number of high-volume item-days stretch the distribution. The view focuses on 0–150 units so the common range remains readable; the caption states how many observations fall outside that visible window.


Show R code
if (data_ready) {
  item_days_above_view <- sum(item_day_data$quantity > 150, na.rm = TRUE)
  max_item_day_quantity <- max(item_day_data$quantity, na.rm = TRUE)

  p_quantity_distribution <- ggplot(item_day_data, aes(x = quantity)) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0, fill = qsr_teal, color = "white", linewidth = 0.25) +
    scale_x_continuous(
      breaks = seq(0, 150, by = 25),
      labels = scales::label_comma(),
      expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))
    ) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 150)) +
    labs(
      x = "Units sold per item-day",
      y = "Number of item-day records",
      caption = paste0(
        "Visible range: 0–150 units. ", scales::comma(item_days_above_view),
        " item-days above 150 are outside the displayed range, not removed from the data. ",
        "Maximum recorded quantity: ", scales::comma(max_item_day_quantity), "."
      )
    ) +
    theme_business

  show_chart(p_quantity_distribution)
} else {
  cat("The histogram will render after the required CSV files are available.")
}









What this tells me: The histogram shows how common quantities are distributed before I compare groups. A long right tail means the average can be pulled upward by a small number of large item-days, so medians and distributions can be helpful alongside means.

title: Exploration
section: Step 3: compare the same outcome across groups
text:
Step 3: compare the same outcome across groups
A group_by() lets me reuse the same outcome summary for each menu category. Total units show the contribution to overall volume; mean and median quantity describe a typical item-day. These answer related but different questions.


Show R code
if (data_ready) {
  category_summary <- item_day_data |>
    group_by(category) |>
    summarise(
      `Total recorded units` = sum(quantity, na.rm = TRUE),
      `Mean units per item-day` = mean(quantity, na.rm = TRUE),
      `Median units per item-day` = median(quantity, na.rm = TRUE),
      `Menu items` = n_distinct(menu_item_id),
      `Item-day records` = n(),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    arrange(desc(`Total recorded units`)) |>
    mutate(
      `Total recorded units` = scales::comma(`Total recorded units`),
      `Mean units per item-day` = scales::number(`Mean units per item-day`, accuracy = 0.1),
      `Median units per item-day` = scales::number(`Median units per item-day`, accuracy = 0.1),
      `Item-day records` = scales::comma(`Item-day records`)
    )

  knitr::kable(
    category_summary,
    caption = "The menu category summary: volume and typical item-day quantity",
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r")
  )
} else {
  cat("The category summary will appear after the required CSV files are available.")
}

What do the promotion groups look like before plotting them?
I also calculate the number of recorded item-days in each promotion group. That matters because group sizes are very different, and a visual difference can be misleading if one group is much smaller than the other.


Show R code
if (data_ready) {
  promotion_summary <- item_day_data |>
    mutate(promotion_status = if_else(is_promotion == 1, "Promotion", "No promotion")) |>
    group_by(promotion_status) |>
    summarise(
      `Item-day records` = n(),
      `Share of records` = 100 * n() / nrow(item_day_data),
      `Mean quantity` = mean(quantity),
      `Median quantity` = median(quantity),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      `Item-day records` = scales::comma(`Item-day records`),
      `Share of records` = paste0(scales::number(`Share of records`, accuracy = 0.1), "%"),
      `Mean quantity` = scales::number(`Mean quantity`, accuracy = 0.1),
      `Median quantity` = scales::number(`Median quantity`, accuracy = 0.1)
    )

    promotion_summary,

title: Exploration
section: Step 4: add calendar context when it helps answer the question
text:
Step 4: add calendar context when it helps answer the question
The raw sales file does not directly say whether an item-day belongs to a weekday, a weekend, or a season. I add those labels from the calendar table with mutate() and case_when(). Then I summarize category units per date. This is important because comparing raw weekday totals with raw weekend totals would be unfair: a typical week contains five weekdays but only two weekend days.


Show R code
if (data_ready) {
  item_day_context <- item_day_data |>
    left_join(
      calendar |> select(date, day_of_week, is_weekend, month, year),
      by = "date"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      day_type = case_when(
        day_of_week %in% c("Saturday", "Sunday") ~ "Weekend",
        TRUE ~ "Weekday"
      ),
      season = case_when(
        month %in% c(12, 1, 2) ~ "Winter",
        month %in% 3:5 ~ "Spring",
        month %in% 6:8 ~ "Summer",
        TRUE ~ "Fall"
      ),
      day_type = factor(day_type, levels = c("Weekday", "Weekend")),
      season = factor(season, levels = c("Winter", "Spring", "Summer", "Fall"))
    )

  category_day <- sales_menu_all |>
    group_by(date, category) |>
    summarise(
      category_units = if (all(is.na(quantity))) NA_real_ else sum(quantity, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    left_join(calendar |> select(date, day_of_week, is_weekend, month, year), by = "date") |>
    mutate(
      day_type = factor(
        if_else(day_of_week %in% c("Saturday", "Sunday"), "Weekend", "Weekday"),
        levels = c("Weekday", "Weekend")
      )
    )

  category_day_summary <- category_day |>
    group_by(category, day_type) |>
    summarise(
      average_daily_category_units = if (all(is.na(category_units))) NA_real_ else mean(category_units, na.rm = TRUE),
      observed_days = sum(!is.na(category_units)),
      .groups = "drop"
    )

  item_summary <- item_day_context |>
    group_by(menu_item_id, menu_item_name, category, unit_price) |>
    summarise(
      total_units = sum(quantity, na.rm = TRUE),
      average_item_day_quantity = mean(quantity, na.rm = TRUE),
      item_days = n(),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    left_join(
      menu_item_details |> select(menu_item_id, prep_minutes),
      by = "menu_item_id"
    )

  safe_correlation <- function(x, y) {
    keep <- complete.cases(x, y)
    if (sum(keep) < 3 || sd(x[keep]) == 0 || sd(y[keep]) == 0) {
      return(NA_real_)
    }
    cor(x[keep], y[keep])
  }

  price_demand_correlation <- safe_correlation(
    item_summary$unit_price,
    item_summary$average_item_day_quantity
  )
  prep_demand_correlation <- safe_correlation(
    item_summary$prep_minutes,
    item_summary$average_item_day_quantity
  )

  # A short sample shows the new calendar labels without printing the whole table.
  item_day_context |>
    select(date, day_of_week, day_type, season, menu_item_name, category, quantity) |>
    arrange(date, menu_item_name) |>
    slice_head(n = 8) |>
    knitr::kable(
      caption = "Example item-day records with the derived calendar labels",
      align = c("l", "l", "l", "l", "l", "l", "r")
    )
} else {
  cat("Calendar grouping and category-day summaries will be created after the required CSV files are available.")
}

title: Exploration
section: Step 5: choose the chart based on the question
text:
Step 5: choose the chart based on the question
A chart is chosen for the job it needs to do. A histogram shows one numeric distribution; grouped bars compare category-level quantities; boxplots and violins reveal how distributions differ; and scatterplots with smoothing lines help check relationships between two numeric variables. These chart types and the use of multiple geoms and facets match the visualization logic covered in Weeks 4–5.

Average daily category demand is useful for comparing weekdays and weekends
Grouped horizontal bars compare categories using the same unit: average category units per calendar day. Averaging by day type makes weekday-versus-weekend comparisons fairer than comparing the raw totals across groups of different sizes.


Show R code
if (data_ready) {
  p_category_daytype <- ggplot(
    category_day_summary |>
      mutate(category = forcats::fct_reorder(category, average_daily_category_units)),
    aes(x = average_daily_category_units, y = category, fill = day_type)
  ) +
    geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.78), width = 0.68) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Weekday" = qsr_teal, "Weekend" = qsr_coral), name = NULL) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.06))) +
    labs(
      x = "Average category units per day",
      y = NULL,
      caption = "Each bar is the average total for one category on a calendar day within that day type."
    ) +
    theme_business +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")

  show_chart(p_category_daytype)
} else {
  cat("The category-by-day-type chart will appear after the required CSV files are available.")
}









What this adds: The chart shows which categories have higher average daily volume on weekdays or weekends. It is a planning clue, not a prediction for any single date.


Category distributions differ, so averages are not the whole story
Violin plots plus boxplots compare numeric quantity across categories, split into weekday and weekend panels. The violin shows where observations concentrate; the boxplot shows the median and middle half of the values. The visible y-range is limited to 0–150 units to make typical observations readable. High values remain in the underlying data and are counted in the caption.


Show R code
if (data_ready) {
  item_days_above_view <- sum(item_day_context$quantity > 150, na.rm = TRUE)

  p_category_distribution <- ggplot(
    item_day_context,
    aes(x = forcats::fct_reorder(category, quantity, .fun = median, na.rm = TRUE),
        y = quantity, fill = category)
  ) +
    geom_violin(trim = TRUE, scale = "width", alpha = 0.42, color = NA) +
    geom_boxplot(width = 0.17, alpha = 0.82, outlier.shape = NA, color = "#203447") +
    facet_wrap(~day_type, nrow = 1) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = category_colors, guide = "none") +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 150, by = 25), labels = scales::label_comma()) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 150)) +
    labs(
      x = NULL,
      y = "Units per item-day",
      caption = paste0(
        "Visible range: 0–150 units. ", scales::comma(item_days_above_view),
        " observations above 150 remain in the analysis but fall outside the displayed range."
      )
    ) +
    theme_business +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1, size = 11), legend.position = "none")

  show_chart(p_category_distribution)
} else {
  cat("The category distribution chart will appear after the required CSV files are available.")
}









What this adds: A category may have high total volume because it contains several popular items, while its typical item-day quantity may still be modest. The distribution view helps distinguish a typical day from the unusually high tail.


Listed price and preparation time do not show a clear overall linear pattern
Two numeric characteristics versus average item-day quantity: scatterplots with linear smoothing lines, split into facets. Each point represents one menu item. The trend lines check for a simple overall association; they do not demonstrate cause and effect.


Show R code
if (data_ready) {
  relationship_data <- item_summary |>
    select(menu_item_name, category, average_item_day_quantity, unit_price, prep_minutes) |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = c(unit_price, prep_minutes),
      names_to = "measure",
      values_to = "x_value"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      measure = recode(
        measure,
        unit_price = "Listed price ($)",
        prep_minutes = "Preparation time (minutes)"
      )
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(x_value), !is.na(average_item_day_quantity))

  p_item_relationships <- ggplot(
    relationship_data,
    aes(x = x_value, y = average_item_day_quantity, color = category)
  ) +
    geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.82) +
    geom_smooth(
      aes(group = 1),
      method = "lm",
      formula = y ~ x,
      se = FALSE,
      color = qsr_coral,
      linewidth = 1.1
    ) +
    facet_wrap(~measure, scales = "free_x", nrow = 1) +
    scale_color_manual(values = category_colors, name = "Category") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(accuracy = 1)) +
    labs(
      x = NULL,
      y = "Average quantity per item-day",
      caption = paste0(
        "Across menu items: price correlation = ", round(price_demand_correlation, 3),
        "; preparation-time correlation = ", round(prep_demand_correlation, 3),
        ". A weak overall linear pattern does not prove that a variable never matters."
      )
    ) +
    theme_business +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")

  show_chart(p_item_relationships)
} else {
  cat("The relationship charts will appear after the required CSV files are available.")
}









What this adds: In this dataset, the overall correlations between listed price or preparation time and average item-day demand are weak. The plots make that lack of a clear linear pattern visible instead of turning every available variable into a headline finding. Category, promotions, and timing may matter in other ways, so these are screening checks rather than final answers.

title: Exploration
text:
What the exploration gives us

The data structure clarifies that quantity is recorded per item-day, while restaurant demand is a daily total.
A small number of large observations can affect averages, so I use distribution views and report the visible range when zooming in.
Category totals and typical item-day quantities answer different questions; both help explain the menu mix.
Day-type comparisons use averages per date rather than raw sums from groups with different numbers of days.
Price and preparation time were checked with scatterplots and smoothing lines, but neither shows a strong overall linear relationship with average item-day quantity in the selected data.

The full report follows these exploratory checks with the deeper business story: which items drive volume, when demand changes, how top products move together, how promotion distributions differ, how volume compares with estimated food-cost margin, and what weather and local events add to the picture.

title: Stage 1 notes
text:
What is not included

Machine learning or a prediction model.
Charts for every possible variable when they do not help answer the business question.
Claims that correlations prove causes or that daily co-movement means two items were bought together.

title: Stage 1 notes
text:
Assumptions to keep visible

Missing sales quantities stay missing in item-level analysis; daily totals use recorded quantities.
The listed price and food-cost values are applied to the entire quantity history only to support a comparison, not historical financial accounting.
Results describe R07 in Minneapolis, not every restaurant in the chain.

title: Quarto guide
text:
Chart display and animation
The graphs are constructed with ggplot2 and rendered as static images. A small local script applies a gentle fade-and-rise reveal when a chart enters the viewport. This is a visual transition only: the graphs do not support hover, zoom, pan, or toolbar actions, and the animation uses no third-party chart library. The analysis and graph code remain in report.qmd and eda.qmd for reproducibility. ## Rendering and sharing
quarto render places the compiled website in _site/. Keep that output and its supporting resource folders together when publishing. The project is configured for a static site deployment; the source CSVs remain local and must not be committed to a public repository. The preview interactive_preview.html is a self-contained reference page, not a replacement for rendering the QMD report against the raw tables.

title: Understanding Restaurant Demand
section: Which menu categories account for the most units?
text:
Which menu categories account for the most units?

This ranking starts with the broad menu mix. It shows where recorded unit volume is concentrated across the five-year period.



Show R code
p_category_demand <- ggplot(
  data = category_demand |> mutate(category = forcats::fct_reorder(category, total_quantity)),
  mapping = aes(x = category, y = total_quantity, fill = category)
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::comma(total_quantity)), hjust = -0.12, size = 4) +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = category_colors, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.17))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Total recorded units") +
  theme_business
show_chart(p_category_demand)










Takeaway: Drinks lead recorded quantity, followed by Burgers, Sides, and Chicken. Volume helps prioritize availability, but it does not show which categories leave the most after food costs.

title: Understanding Restaurant Demand
text:
Which individual products stand out?

The category ranking can hide individual best sellers. This chart ranks the ten menu items with the highest total recorded quantity.



Show R code
p_top_items <- ggplot(
  data = top_items |> mutate(menu_item_name = forcats::fct_reorder(menu_item_name, total_quantity)),
  mapping = aes(x = menu_item_name, y = total_quantity, fill = category)
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::comma(total_quantity)), hjust = -0.12, size = 3.7) +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = category_colors, name = "Category") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Total recorded units") +
  theme_business
show_chart(p_top_items)










Takeaway: Soft Drink Regular, French Fries Regular, and Classic Cheeseburger lead individual-item demand. These products are sensible starting points for availability and replenishment checks during busy periods.

title: Understanding Restaurant Demand
section: Which months have the strongest average daily demand?
text:
Which months have the strongest average daily demand?

A line chart is appropriate for the ordered months. It shows the recurring seasonal rhythm without plotting every daily fluctuation.



Show R code
p_monthly_demand <- ggplot(month_summary, aes(x = month_label, y = average_daily_demand, group = 1)) +
  geom_line(color = qsr_teal, linewidth = 1.25) +
  geom_point(color = qsr_coral, size = 3.4) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Average daily recorded units") +
  theme_business
show_chart(p_monthly_demand)










Takeaway: Demand peaks in Jul and is lowest in Jan. The recurring pattern can guide seasonal preparation and stock reviews, but it is not a guarantee for an individual day.

title: Understanding Restaurant Demand
section: Do categories follow the same seasonal pattern?
text:
Do categories follow the same seasonal pattern?

The overall line hides category differences. Each panel below shows average daily category quantity by month, using the same month order and a separate vertical scale for readability.



Show R code
p_category_month <- ggplot(category_month, aes(x = month_label, y = average_daily_category_units, group = 1)) +
  geom_line(color = qsr_teal, linewidth = 1.0) +
  geom_point(color = qsr_coral, size = 2.3) +
  facet_wrap(vars(category), scales = "free_y", ncol = 4) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Average daily category units",
       caption = "Panels use separate y-axes: compare each category's shape, not the height across panels.") +
  theme_business +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12), axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10.5), panel.spacing = grid::unit(1.1, "lines"))
show_chart(p_category_month)










Takeaway: The small multiples show whether categories share the overall summer pattern or differ in timing. This helps avoid assuming that every product group needs the same seasonal plan.

title: Understanding Restaurant Demand
section: Are the busiest weekdays consistently busy?
text:
Are the busiest weekdays consistently busy?

A boxplot compares the distribution of total daily units across weekdays. Unlike averages alone, it also shows the median, spread, and unusually high or low days.



Show R code
p_weekday_distribution <- ggplot(daily_context, aes(x = day_of_week, y = daily_demand)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#CFE5E8", color = qsr_teal, outlier.alpha = 0.45, linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Daily recorded units") +
  theme_business +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
show_chart(p_weekday_distribution)










Takeaway: Use the full spread of past days, not only the average weekday, when discussing staffing and preparation. Weekend patterns are useful planning context, but busy and quiet days still vary within each weekday.

title: Understanding Restaurant Demand
section: Which high-volume products share similar daily patterns?
text:
Which high-volume products share similar daily patterns?

A correlation heatmap compares daily quantities for the eight highest-volume items. It is a discovery tool: positive values indicate that two items tend to rise and fall together, while values near zero indicate little overall linear co-movement.



Show R code
p_product_correlation <- ggplot(product_cor_long, aes(x = item_x, y = item_y, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = number(correlation, accuracy = 0.01)), size = 3.8, color = "#203447") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#3C7DA4", mid = "#F6F8FA", high = "#D96D5B", midpoint = 0,
                       limits = c(-1, 1), name = "Pearson r") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = function(x) stringr::str_wrap(x, width = 18)) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) stringr::str_wrap(x, width = 18)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "Based on matched daily observations. Shared weekends or seasonal changes can contribute to co-movement.") +
  theme_business +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1, size = 10.5), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10.5),
        panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "right", plot.margin = margin(12, 24, 24, 12))
show_chart(p_product_correlation)










Takeaway: The heatmap helps identify product pairs worth a closer look. It measures similar daily patterns, not whether customers bought the products together on the same transaction.

title: Understanding Restaurant Demand
section: Does the strongest product pair show a clear pattern?
text:
Does the strongest product pair show a clear pattern?

The scatterplot follows up on the strongest absolute correlation in the heatmap. Each point is one day with recorded quantities for both products; the line summarizes their overall linear relationship.

The pair selected from the current data is Soft Drink Regular and Soft Drink Large (Pearson r = 0.58).


Show R code
p_product_pair <- ggplot(product_pair_data, aes(x = .data[[product_a]], y = .data[[product_b]])) +
  geom_point(color = qsr_teal, alpha = 0.25, size = 1.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE, color = qsr_coral, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(x = paste("Daily units:", product_a), y = paste("Daily units:", product_b),
       caption = "Association does not establish that one product causes demand for the other.") +
  theme_business
show_chart(p_product_pair)










Takeaway: The points and smoothing line show whether the selected pair has a consistent pattern or substantial scatter. Treat this as a replenishment-planning clue, not evidence of customer-level product bundling.

title: Understanding Restaurant Demand
section: Compare volume with estimated food-cost margin
text:
Compare volume with estimated food-cost margin

The horizontal position shows average item-day demand by category, the vertical position shows average listed unit margin, and bubble size represents estimated total food-cost margin. This puts volume and simple economics in one view.



Show R code
p_category_economics <- ggplot(category_economics, aes(x = average_item_day_quantity, y = average_unit_margin, size = estimated_total_margin, color = category)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.82) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = category), size = 4, box.padding = 0.45, point.padding = 0.4,
                           max.overlaps = Inf, show.legend = FALSE, seed = 42) +
  scale_color_manual(values = category_colors, guide = "none") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(5, 18), labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M", accuracy = 0.1),
                        name = "Estimated total margin") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = number_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  labs(x = "Average units per item-day", y = "Average listed margin per unit",
       caption = "Estimated margin = observed quantity × (listed price − listed food cost). This is not net profit.") +
  theme_business +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

title: Understanding Restaurant Demand
section: Does the temperature-demand relationship remain within seasons?
text:
Does the temperature-demand relationship remain within seasons?

The overall correlation is strong, but both temperature and demand vary through the year. Faceted scatterplots let us see whether the relationship looks similar within Winter, Spring, Summer, and Fall.

The overall Pearson correlation between daily demand and average temperature is 0.76. The panels below provide context for that overall value.


Show R code
p_temperature_season <- ggplot(
  data = daily_context |> filter(!is.na(avg_temp_f), !is.na(daily_demand)),
  mapping = aes(x = avg_temp_f, y = daily_demand)
) +
  geom_point(color = qsr_teal, alpha = 0.22, size = 1.35) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = qsr_coral, linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(vars(season), ncol = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "Average daily temperature (°F)", y = "Daily recorded units",
       caption = "Seasonal patterns may explain part of the overall association; the lines are descriptive, not causal.") +
  theme_business +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13), panel.spacing = grid::unit(1.25, "lines"))
show_chart(p_temperature_season)

title: Understanding Restaurant Demand
section: Which local events coincide with higher demand?
text:
Which local events coincide with higher demand?

This comparison places each named event beside regular days. Values at the bar ends show average daily units and how many days contribute to each average.



Show R code
p_event_comparison <- ggplot(
  data = event_summary |> mutate(event_group = forcats::fct_reorder(event_group, average_daily_demand)),
  mapping = aes(x = event_group, y = average_daily_demand, fill = baseline_type)
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(comma(round(average_daily_demand)), " units/day · ", comma(days), " days")),
            hjust = -0.08, size = 3.7) +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Regular day" = "#8E9AA5", "Local event" = qsr_teal), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.28))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Average daily recorded units") +
  theme_business
show_chart(p_event_comparison)










Takeaway: Three named event groups exceed the regular-day average; Winter Carnival is slightly below it. Use the event calendar as a planning signal, not a promise that all events raise demand.

title: Understanding Restaurant Demand
section: Do listed price or preparation time show a clear relationship with average demand?
text:
Do listed price or preparation time show a clear relationship with average demand?

Each point is one menu item. The two scatterplots test whether average item-day quantity follows a clear linear pattern with listed price or preparation time. Points are colored by menu category, and the line summarizes the overall trend.



Show R code
p_price_demand <- ggplot(item_summary, aes(x = unit_price, y = average_item_day_quantity, color = category)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = qsr_coral, linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = category_colors, name = "Category") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Listed price per item", y = "Average units per item-day") +
  theme_business
show_chart(p_price_demand)










Does preparation time relate to average demand?

Each point is one menu item. The trend line helps check whether items that take longer to prepare also tend to have higher or lower average item-day demand.



Show R code
p_prep_demand <- ggplot(item_summary, aes(x = prep_minutes, y = average_item_day_quantity, color = category)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = qsr_coral, linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = category_colors, name = "Category") +
  labs(x = "Preparation time (minutes)", y = "Average units per item-day") +
  theme_business
show_chart(p_prep_demand)









The linear correlations are -0.01 for listed price and 0.08 for preparation time.

Takeaway: These plots do not show a clear overall linear relationship between either listed price or preparation time and average item-day quantity across the 50 menu items. That is useful context, but it does not prove these factors never matter for a specific item.

title: Understanding Restaurant Demand
section: Does monthly advertising spend move with demand?
text:
Does monthly advertising spend move with demand?

The monthly scatterplot tests the relationship between local advertising spend and average daily demand. Colors distinguish years so we can see whether the pattern is spread across the five-year period.



Show R code
p_marketing_demand <- ggplot(
  data = monthly_marketing |> filter(!is.na(local_ad_spend_usd), !is.na(monthly_average_daily_demand)),
  mapping = aes(x = local_ad_spend_usd, y = monthly_average_daily_demand, color = year)
) +
  geom_point(size = 2.9, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = qsr_coral, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = "Year") +
  labs(x = "Monthly local advertising spend", y = "Average daily recorded units",
       caption = paste0("Monthly advertising-spend correlation = ", round(ad_spend_correlation, 2),
                        ". Seasonal demand and planned spending may explain part of this association.")) +
  theme_business
show_chart(p_marketing_demand)










Takeaway: Advertising spend and demand move together in the raw monthly data, but this does not show that advertising caused higher demand. A planned test or a comparison that accounts for seasonality would be needed to estimate impact. Social-post count and precipitation have weak simple correlations with demand, so they are not given separate headline charts.

title: Understanding Restaurant Demand
text:
Final thought
The useful story is not simply what sold the most. Demand has a seasonal rhythm, products show different patterns, and high unit volume is not the same as high estimated food-cost margin. The best next decisions combine these findings and use new tests where the current data cannot establish a clear relationship.

title: Data used in this analysis
text:
This analysis focuses on R07 in Minneapolis and daily menu-item sales from 2021–2025. The eight source tables below are the ones needed to answer the selected business questions.
restaurant_profile.csv is part of the supplied bundle, but it is not needed for the Stage 1 questions selected here.

title: Data used in this analysis
text:
How the tables connect
Sales joins to the menu by menu_item_id and to the calendar by date. Weather connects by the restaurant city and date; events connect by restaurant and date; food cost and preparation time connect by menu_item_id; marketing connects by restaurant, year, and month.

title: Data used in this analysis
text:
Data-quality findings
The checks below look for missing sales quantities, duplicate item-day records, unmatched menu details, invalid temperature codes, and gaps in weather coverage. The results are calculated from the original CSV files when the page is rendered.


Show R code used for the data-quality checks
library(tidyverse)
source("R/load_data.R")
missing_inputs <- qsr_missing_files("data")

if (length(missing_inputs) > 0) {
  cat(
    "The data-quality table will appear after the eight original CSV files are copied into data/. Missing files: ",
    paste(missing_inputs, collapse = ", ")
  )
} else {
  qsr_data <- load_qsr_data("data")

  sales_r07 <- qsr_data$sales |>
    mutate(date = as.Date(date)) |>
    filter(restaurant_id == "R07")
  menu_items <- qsr_data$menu_items
  calendar <- qsr_data$calendar |> mutate(date = as.Date(date))
  weather <- qsr_data$weather |> mutate(date = as.Date(date))
  menu_item_details <- qsr_data$menu_item_details
  r07_city <- qsr_data$restaurants |>
    filter(restaurant_id == "R07") |>
    pull(city) |>
    first()

  missing_quantity_n <- sum(is.na(sales_r07$quantity))
  missing_quantity_pct <- 100 * missing_quantity_n / nrow(sales_r07)

  duplicate_item_days_n <- sales_r07 |>
    count(date, menu_item_id) |>
    filter(n > 1) |>
    nrow()

  sales_with_menu <- sales_r07 |>
    left_join(
      menu_items |> select(menu_item_id, menu_item_name, category),
      by = "menu_item_id"
    )
  unmatched_menu_rows_n <- sum(
    is.na(sales_with_menu$menu_item_name) | is.na(sales_with_menu$category)
  )

  weather_r07 <- weather |> filter(city == r07_city)
  invalid_temp_n <- sum(weather_r07$avg_temp_f == -99, na.rm = TRUE)
  weather_dates_missing_n <- calendar |>
    distinct(date) |>
    anti_join(weather_r07 |> distinct(date), by = "date") |>
    nrow()

  missing_price_n <- sum(is.na(menu_items$unit_price))
  missing_food_cost_n <- sum(is.na(menu_item_details$food_cost_per_unit))
  missing_prep_n <- sum(is.na(menu_item_details$prep_minutes))

  result_count <- function(n, label) {
    if (n == 0) "None found" else paste0(scales::comma(n), " ", label)
  }

  quality_findings <- tibble(
    Finding = c(
      "Missing sales quantities",
      "Duplicate date + menu-item combinations",
      "Sales rows missing a menu name or category after joining",
      "Temperature values coded as -99",
      "Calendar dates without a matching weather record for R07's city",
      "Missing listed menu prices",
      "Missing food-cost values",
      "Missing preparation-time values"
    ),
    Result = c(
      paste0(scales::comma(missing_quantity_n), " (", scales::number(missing_quantity_pct, accuracy = 0.1), "%)"),
      result_count(duplicate_item_days_n, "duplicate date-item combinations"),
      result_count(unmatched_menu_rows_n, "unmatched sales rows"),
      result_count(invalid_temp_n, "temperature values coded as -99"),
      result_count(weather_dates_missing_n, "calendar dates without a weather record"),
      result_count(missing_price_n, "menu items missing a listed price"),
      result_count(missing_food_cost_n, "menu items missing food cost"),
      result_count(missing_prep_n, "menu items missing preparation time")
    ),
    `How it is handled` = c(
      "Exclude from item-day comparisons. Daily totals use recorded quantities, so totals may be understated on affected dates.",
      if (duplicate_item_days_n == 0) "No duplicate item-day rows needed to be removed." else "Review duplicate rows before interpreting item-day totals.",
      if (unmatched_menu_rows_n == 0) "The sales-to-menu join matches the required item descriptions and categories." else "Review unmatched item IDs before category or product comparisons.",
      "Treat -99 as a missing temperature, not as a real weather reading.",
      "Do not invent weather values; weather comparisons use dates with matching observations.",
      if (missing_price_n == 0) "No price-related exclusions are required." else "Items without price are omitted from analyses that require listed price.",
      if (missing_food_cost_n == 0) "No food-cost exclusions are required." else "Items without food cost cannot contribute to estimated food-cost margin.",
      if (missing_prep_n == 0) "No preparation-time exclusions are required." else "Items without preparation time are omitted from preparation-time comparisons."
    )
  )

  knitr::kable(
    quality_findings,
    caption = "Data-quality checks and how the analysis handles each finding",
    col.names = c("Finding", "Result", "How the analysis handles it"),
    align = c("l", "l", "l")
  )
}

The initial review of this dataset found 365 missing sales quantities (about 0.4% of sales rows), no duplicate date-and-menu-item combinations, 14 weather temperatures coded as -99, and 55 calendar dates without a matching weather record for Minneapolis. The checks above recalculate these results from the source files whenever the site is rendered.






Note



Not every blank field is an error. For example, holiday_name is normally blank on non-holidays, and an event name is blank on days without a special event. Missing sales quantities and invalid temperature codes need explicit handling because they can affect analysis.

title: QSR Daily Demand
text:
What sells?

Drinks lead total recorded units.
Soft Drink Regular, French Fries Regular, and Classic Cheeseburger are among the leading individual items.
Category and item rankings help focus stock checks.

Business implication: Start operational planning with the products that account for much of the recorded volume.

title: QSR Daily Demand
text:
When does demand change?

Average daily demand is strongest in Jul and lowest in Jan.
Category-specific monthly lines help show whether every menu group follows the same pattern.
Weekday boxplots add the variation hidden by averages.

Business implication: Use historical demand as a starting point for staffing and preparation—not as a guarantee for a particular day.

title: QSR Daily Demand
text:
What relationships did we examine?

A correlation heatmap and follow-up scatterplot compare daily patterns for high-volume products.
Violin/boxplots compare promotional and non-promotional distributions by category.
Scatterplots test price and preparation time against average item-day quantity.
Faceted temperature plots and event comparisons add external context.

Interpretation: Correlation does not prove causation. Product co-movement is not proof of same-transaction purchases.

title: QSR Daily Demand
text:
Volume is not value

Drinks lead units.
Burgers lead estimated total food-cost margin, followed by Combos and Chicken.
The estimate uses listed price and food cost across the full history; it is not net profit.

Business implication: Consider demand and unit economics together.

title: QSR Daily Demand
text:
What should happen next?

Protect availability of core items.
Plan for seasonal and weekday variation.
Evaluate promotions by category and compare like with like.
Prepare for specific local events.
Use follow-up tests before attributing changes to advertising or weather.







Note



Stage 1 ends with descriptive analysis and business recommendations. No machine-learning model is included.

title: QSR Daily Demand
text:
The story in brief
What sells: drinks and a small group of familiar items account for much of the recorded volume.
When it sells: demand rises into summer, and daily patterns vary by weekday and category.
What is worth testing: promotions differ by category; weather and marketing show associations that need careful interpretation; price and preparation time show little overall linear relationship with average item-day quantity.
The report uses the graph types covered in Weeks 1–5, including ranking bars, lines, distributions, scatterplots, correlation displays, and faceting. It stays within descriptive analysis and does not add machine learning.
